title: 1 Samuel 27:8–12
context: From Ziklag David raids peoples to the south and leaves no survivors who could report him, while telling Achish he has raided Judah’s territory. The narrator records the raids and the deception without explicit comment, and Achish believes him.

verses.text: David and his men went up and raided the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites; for those were the inhabitants of the land who were of old, on the way to Shur, even to the land of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: David and his men raid the Geshurites, Girzites, and Amalekites, ancient inhabitants toward Shur and Egypt. Arminian readers see David attacking peoples outside Israel rather than his own countrymen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the targets are not Judean towns. Amalek is already marked for judgment in chapter 15, and the Geshurites appear among unconquered peoples in Joshua 13:2, though the narrator does not evaluate this raid.

verses.text: David struck the land, and saved no man or woman alive, and took away the sheep, the cattle, the donkeys, the camels, and the clothing. Then he returned, and came to Achish.
verses.arminianNotes: David “saved no man or woman alive” and takes the livestock and clothing before returning to Achish. Arminian readers note the grim report and the narrator’s silence about whether God commanded these raids.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the verse soberly and observe that the text does not present the raids as an instruction from God. Readers in both traditions differ on how far David’s actions here should be judged or explained.

verses.text: Achish said, “Against whom have you made a raid today?” David said, “Against the South of Judah, against the South of the Jerahmeelites, and against the South of the Kenites.”
verses.arminianNotes: Achish asks, “Against whom have you made a raid today?” David answers, “Against the South of Judah.” Arminian readers see deliberate deception that keeps Achish trusting him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see David misleading his host. The narrator reports the deceit plainly, and both traditions generally read biblical narrative as recording such acts without thereby approving them.

verses.text: David saved neither man nor woman alive to bring them to Gath, saying, “Lest they should tell about us, saying, ‘David did this, and this has been his way all the time he has lived in the country of the Philistines.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: David leaves no one alive, “Lest they should tell about us.” Arminian readers see the deception leading to further violence, showing how one concealment can require another.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the human cost of maintaining the cover story. The narrator states David’s motive directly, letting readers weigh the moral weight of the choice without softening it.

verses.text: Achish believed David, saying, “He has made his people Israel utterly to abhor him. Therefore he will be my servant forever.”
verses.arminianNotes: Achish believes David, saying, “He has made his people Israel utterly to abhor him.” Arminian readers see the irony that Achish trusts David most when he is most mistaken about him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the deception succeed for now. Achish’s expectation that David “will be my servant forever” sets up the crisis of loyalty that chapters 28 and 29 bring to a head.
